title: Woke up extremely breathless: a 75-year-old smoker with COPD
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 75-year-old retired plumber with COPD. He was brought to the ED by ambulance after waking extremely breathless, with wheeze and a new yellow cough. The candidate then interprets his observations, arterial blood gas, bloods and chest X-ray. They diagnose an infective exacerbation of COPD with compensated hypercapnia, weigh the differentials (pneumonia, pneumothorax, PE, cardiac causes and lung cancer), outline ED management with controlled oxygen, and safety-net for discharge.
focus: Acute breathlessness in an older smoker with COPD: eliciting the features of an infective exacerbation, excluding the dangerous differentials, reading the blood gas and chest X-ray, and managing the exacerbation with controlled oxygen
stem: You are a final-year medical student on your Emergency Department placement at a metropolitan hospital. It is mid-morning. Shawn Peters, a 75-year-old man, has been brought in by ambulance with shortness of breath. He is in an acute bay on a cardiac monitor, on oxygen through nasal prongs, with an IV cannula in place. A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions. The nurse has taken his observations and recorded an ECG. Bloods and an arterial blood gas have been sent and a chest X-ray has been requested. The ED registrar has asked you to see him first.
tasks: Take a focused history from Shawn and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, arterial blood gas, blood results and chest X-ray report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Shawn Peters, a 75-year-old retired plumber. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. You are sitting bolt upright on the trolley, leaning forward with your hands on your knees, breathing out through pursed lips. You are on oxygen through nasal prongs. You speak in short sentences and stop to catch your breath. You are frightened but cooperative. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (when the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Shawn came in by ambulance about 20 minutes ago. When the paramedics got to him his resp rate was 32 and his sats were 86% on room air, heart rate 114. They gave him salbutamol and put him on 2 litres by nasal prongs. At triage he was resp rate 26, sats 92% on 2 litres, heart rate 108 and regular, BP 148/84, temp 37.8, BGL 9.6. The repeat just now is about the same: resp rate 26, sats 92%, heart rate 106, BP 146/84. The ECG is done, bloods and a gas have gone, and the X-ray has been requested."

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they ask about the oxygen, the nurse asks, "What saturation are you aiming for?" A target of 88 to 92% means the oxygen stays as it is.
  • If they ask for more oxygen, a face mask or a target of 94% or higher, the nurse asks, "He has COPD. Are you sure?" If they go ahead anyway, after a few minutes you become a little drowsy and slow to answer, and the nurse says, "His sats are 98%, but he's getting sleepy." Turning the oxygen back down to the 88 to 92% target settles this.
  • If they order a bronchodilator, the nurse asks for the dose and route and gives it. A few minutes later you say, "That's a bit easier."
  • If they try to lie you flat, say: "I can't lie down. I need to sit up to breathe."
  • If they ask about the ECG, the nurse says: "Sinus tach at about 106. The registrar glanced at it and said there's nothing acute."
  • If they ask for any other results now, the examiner says these will be given in Part 2.
  • If they explain calmly what they are doing, you settle a little. If they use jargon, ask what it means.

Opening line: "I woke up this morning... feeling extremely out of breath."

History (give only when asked; short sentences):

The breathlessness

  • Onset and course: you have felt unwell since last night. You woke this morning extremely out of breath, much worse than last night.
  • Character: "Feels like there's a tight band around my chest. I could only take very shallow breaths, and it was hard getting air in."
  • Severity: you could not walk to the toilet this morning. "Normally I get breathless walking to the letterbox but manage around the house."
  • Previous episodes: "It was a horrible feeling. I've never had anything like this before."
  • What helped: "The doctors in the ambulance put me on oxygen and gave me a puff of some medication, which helped a bit."
  • Who found you: "I was lucky my son was in the room next door." He had stayed the night and called the ambulance.

Chest symptoms (only if asked)

  • Wheeze: yes, you have been wheezy since last night.
  • Cough: you always have a dry smoker's cough. Since last night you have been bringing up yellow phlegm. Not green. No blood.
  • Fever: you feel a little hot and sweaty. You did not take your temperature. No shaking or shivering attacks.
  • Tiredness: generally tired since last night.
  • The tightness: "It's not a pain exactly. It's tight, like I can't get the air in." It is not sharp, and it is not worse when you breathe in.

Other symptoms (only if asked; all of these are no)

  • No high fevers or rigors. No sharp pain on breathing in. No one around you has been sick.
  • You have not been more breathless lying flat in recent weeks. You do not wake at night gasping. Your ankles are not swollen. No pink frothy spit.
  • No coughing up blood. No pain or swelling in either calf. You have not been laid up in bed and have not travelled.
  • No central crushing chest pain, nothing going to your arm or jaw. No nausea. No palpitations.
  • No night sweats, no weight loss, and your appetite is normal.

Past medical history

  • COPD, diagnosed 8 years ago. You have never had a flare-up like this. You have never been in hospital for your lungs and never needed a breathing machine.
  • High blood pressure.
  • High cholesterol.
  • Type 2 diabetes.
  • A heart attack in 2017, treated with a stent.

Medications (you are not sure of the doses: "My son has the list.")

  • Ramipril, metoprolol, atorvastatin, aspirin.
  • Apixaban, a blood thinner. Your heart doctor started it. If asked why you take it, say: "My son says it's for an irregular heartbeat they found a couple of years ago." (This is paroxysmal atrial fibrillation; your heartbeat is regular today.)
  • Metformin.
  • Salbutamol (the blue puffer) when needed, and tiotropium once a day.
  • You have been taking them all.

Allergies: none that you know of.

Family history

  • Your father died of end-stage kidney disease.
  • Your mother had lung cancer.

Social history

  • Home: you live alone. Your wife died last year of a coronavirus infection.
  • Function: independent. Your son is your main carer and visits often.
  • Smoking: one pack a day since your early 20s. You tried to quit, but started again after your wife died.
  • Alcohol: none. No recreational drugs.
  • Work: retired plumber. If asked about dust or asbestos: not that you know of.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think your lungs have "packed up". It was the most frightening thing you have ever been through. You are scared because you live alone and only got help because your son happened to be there. You want to be able to breathe again.

If the candidate asks whether anything else is worrying you, say: "I'm not sure if I can cope with another episode of this."

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: older man sitting upright and leaning forward (tripod position), with pursed-lip breathing. Using his neck and shoulder muscles to breathe. Speaking in short sentences. Not cyanosed on oxygen. Alert and answering appropriately. Smells of cigarettes.
  • Vital signs: as the nurse reported. Temperature 37.8 °C.
  • Hands: heavy tar staining of the right index and middle fingers. No clubbing. Warm, capillary refill 2 seconds. No flapping tremor.
  • Face: no central cyanosis on oxygen. Pursed-lip breathing.
  • Pulse: 106/min, regular, normal volume.
  • Blood pressure: 146/84.
  • JVP: not raised. It is hard to see because of his neck muscle use.
  • Trachea: central. Cricosternal distance reduced to 2 finger-breadths. Tracheal tug present.
  • Chest inspection: barrel-shaped chest with an increased front-to-back diameter. No scars.
  • Palpation: expansion reduced but equal on both sides. Apex beat hard to feel.
  • Percussion: hyper-resonant throughout both sides. Loss of the normal cardiac dullness.
  • Auscultation: breath sounds reduced throughout both lungs, with a prolonged expiratory phase. Widespread expiratory polyphonic wheeze on both sides. A few coarse crackles at both bases that change after coughing. No bronchial breathing, no focal crackles, vocal resonance equal, no pleural rub.
  • Heart: heart sounds soft, dual, no murmurs, no third heart sound.
  • Legs: no ankle or sacral oedema. Calves soft and non-tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Shawn's identity and asks whether he is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.

Acts on the nurse's report before finishing the history: keeps Shawn upright, states a controlled oxygen target of SpO2 88 to 92% rather than increasing the oxygen, and keeps questions short and mostly closed because he is breathless.
check.d: Credit when the 88 to 92% target is stated. Do not credit asking for high-flow oxygen or a mask to 'normal' saturations.

check.x: History
Characterises the breathlessness:
check.d: Credit when onset and at least 2 of the other 3 are elicited.

kids.x: Onset and course: unwell since last night, woke this morning extremely breathless, much worse this morning
Character: a tight band around the chest, only shallow breaths, hard to get air in; never had anything like this before
Severity: cannot walk to the toilet, when normally he is breathless walking to the letterbox but manages around the house
Response: the paramedics' oxygen and inhaled medicine helped a bit

check.x: Elicits the features of an exacerbation: wheeze, his usual dry smoker's cough now bringing up yellow sputum, no haemoptysis, feeling hot and sweaty, and generalised fatigue since last night.
check.d: Credit when the change in sputum and at least 2 others are elicited.

check.x: Asks about symptoms of the differentials (all absent):
check.d: Credit when at least 4 of the 5 are explored, which must include PE and ACS.

kids.x: Pneumonia: high fever, rigors, pleuritic pain, sick contacts
Heart failure: orthopnoea, PND, leg swelling, pink frothy sputum
PE: pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, immobility, calf pain or swelling
ACS: central chest pain, radiation to the arm or jaw, nausea, palpitations
Constitutional (malignancy): night sweats, weight loss, appetite

check.x: Takes the past medical history: COPD for 8 years with no previous exacerbations, admissions or ventilation; hypertension, dyslipidaemia, type 2 diabetes, and an MI with a coronary stent in 2017.
check.d: Credit when the COPD history (including no previous admissions) and the MI are elicited, plus at least 2 others.

check.x: Takes the medication and allergy history: ramipril, metoprolol, atorvastatin, aspirin, apixaban, metformin, salbutamol and tiotropium; no known allergies.
check.d: Credit when at least 6 are named, including apixaban and both inhalers, and allergies are asked about.

check.x: Takes a family history: father died of end-stage kidney disease; mother had lung cancer.
Quantifies smoking: a pack a day since his early 20s (about 50 or more pack-years), current smoker, restarted after his wife died.
Takes the rest of the social history: lives alone, wife died last year of a coronavirus infection, independent, son is his main carer and visits often, no alcohol, retired plumber.
check.d: Credit when at least 4 are covered, including living alone.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations and responds with empathy: frightened, never had anything like this, lucky his son was next door, not sure he can cope with another episode.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs: tripod position, pursed-lip breathing, accessory muscle use, speaking in short sentences, cyanosis, temperature 37.8 °C, and the nurse's observations.
Respiratory examination:
check.d: Credit when percussion and auscultation are both performed and compared side to side.

kids.x: Hands and face: tar staining, no clubbing, no CO2 retention flap, no central cyanosis
Inspection and palpation: barrel chest, reduced cricosternal distance, trachea central, expansion reduced but symmetrical
Reduced air entry with prolonged expiration and widespread expiratory wheeze; coarse basal crackles that change with coughing; no bronchial breathing or focal signs

check.x: Looks for heart failure and DVT: JVP not raised, no third heart sound, no ankle or sacral oedema, calves soft and non-tender.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: red zone RR and SpO2 on room air at the scene. Improved, but RR and SpO2 still in the yellow zone on 2 L/min, needing a clinical review. SpO2 92% is already at the top of his target, so the oxygen should not be increased. Low-grade temperature; not shocked.
check.d: Credit when the ED RR and SpO2 are identified as yellow zone needing review and SpO2 92% is recognised as the top of his target; the scene values are not required.

check.x: Interprets the ABG: hypoxaemia on oxygen (PaO2 64) and hypercapnia (PaCO2 52) with a normal pH and raised bicarbonate. This means compensated chronic hypercapnic (type 2) respiratory failure with no acute respiratory acidosis, so NIV is not needed now but controlled oxygen is essential.
check.d: Credit when the hypercapnia, the normal pH and the implication for the oxygen target are all stated.

check.x: Interprets the bloods: neutrophilia and CRP 42 (infection or inflammation); first hs-troponin below the 99th percentile (against ACS; repeat at 2 to 3 hours per the ACS pathway); normal renal function; raised glucose (known diabetes, will rise with corticosteroids); normal Hb.
check.d: Credit when raised WCC/CRP and the first troponin below the 99th percentile are interpreted.

check.x: Reads the chest X-ray:
check.d: Credit when hyperinflation is described and consolidation and pneumothorax are both excluded.

kids.x: Hyperinflation: more than 6 anterior ribs, flattened hemidiaphragms, narrow heart
No pulmonary oedema, effusion or mass

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as an infective exacerbation of COPD. Justifies it with a subacute course, wheeze, yellow sputum, feeling hot, a heavy smoking history, partial relief from the inhaled bronchodilator, widespread wheeze, raised WCC and CRP, and no consolidation.
check.d: Credit when at least 4 supporting features are given.

check.x: Names differentials with a feature from this patient for or against each: pneumonia, pneumothorax, PE, a cardiac cause (heart failure or ACS) and lung cancer.
check.d: Credit when at least 3 are named, each with a patient feature.

check.x: Management

Escalates to the ED registrar with continuous monitoring, keeps him upright, and gives controlled oxygen titrated to SpO2 88 to 92% (nasal prongs or Venturi), with bronchodilators by spacer or air-driven nebuliser.

Gives short-acting bronchodilators: salbutamol 400 to 800 micrograms (4 to 8 puffs) by MDI and spacer, or 2.5 to 5 mg nebulised, repeated as needed, with ipratropium 4 to 8 puffs (21 micrograms per puff) by MDI and spacer, or 500 micrograms nebulised (air-driven), repeated as needed (tiotropium withheld while ipratropium is given regularly).
check.d: Credit salbutamol with a correct dose by one route and ipratropium with a correct dose by one route; withholding tiotropium is not required.

check.x: Prescribes prednisolone 30 to 50 mg orally once daily for 5 days and plans blood glucose monitoring because he has type 2 diabetes.

Gives an oral antibiotic for the purulent sputum (amoxicillin 500 mg 8-hourly for 5 days, or doxycycline 200 mg on day 1 then 100 mg daily for 4 days), sends sputum for microscopy and culture, and sends a nasopharyngeal respiratory viral PCR (SARS-CoV-2, influenza, RSV) with droplet precautions until resulted.
check.d: Credit either antibiotic with a correct dose and duration; sputum culture and viral PCR are not required.

check.x: Plans a repeat ABG within about an hour, or sooner if he becomes drowsy. States that NIV is indicated if pH falls below 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 mmHg despite treatment, with ICU or HDU involvement if he worsens.

Admits him under general medicine or respiratory. Continues his regular medicines (except tiotropium while regular ipratropium is given), including apixaban and metoprolol, but withholds metformin while he is acutely unwell and hypoxaemic (restart once recovered and eating normally), with BGL monitoring and correctional insulin for steroid-induced hyperglycaemia. Offers NRT in hospital. Involves physiotherapy, OT and social work, and his son, because he lives alone.
check.d: Credit when admission is stated with at least 1 of the other parts.

check.x: Safety netting

Answers Shawn's concerns in plain words: an infection set off a flare-up of his COPD; a written COPD action plan, inhaler technique and quitting smoking all lower the chance of another one. Raises smoking with empathy for his grief.

Tells Shawn in plain words to call 000 if he is too breathless to speak, the reliever does not help, his lips go blue, he becomes drowsy or confused, or he has chest pain. He should see his GP the same day if his sputum changes colour or increases, he gets a fever, or he needs his reliever more often.

Arranges follow-up: GP review within 7 days of discharge, a pulmonary rehabilitation referral, spirometry when stable, vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, RSV), Quitline, and support at home (his son, a personal alarm, bereavement support).
check.d: Credit when GP review within 7 days and pulmonary rehabilitation are arranged.

part2.lead: Here are his observations, his arterial blood gas, his blood results and the chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
Ask this only after the examiner reads question 4:

  • "Will this happen again? I'm not sure I can cope with another one... and do I really have to give up the smokes?"

If the candidate acknowledges your grief before talking about smoking, you say you will think about it and would take the patches. If they lecture you, go quiet. If they use jargon, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: The first set was taken by the paramedics on room air before treatment. The ED sets are on 2 L/min nasal prongs, after the paramedics gave salbutamol. Temperature was not measured at the scene.
handover.model:
• Read: at the scene on room air, RR 32 and SpO2 86% were in the red zone, with HR 114 (white) and BP 156/90. In ED on 2 L/min, RR 26 and SpO2 92% are in the yellow zone. HR 108 then 106, BP 148/84 and temperature 37.8 °C are white, and BGL is 9.6.
  • Meaning: severe tachypnoea and hypoxaemia before treatment. He has improved with salbutamol and controlled oxygen but still needs oxygen and is tachypnoeic. The low-grade temperature fits infection. He is not shocked.
  • Changes: the yellow zone calls for a clinical review, here a senior ED review now. SpO2 92% is already at the top of his 88 to 92% target, so do not increase the oxygen. The team should document altered calling criteria for his SpO2. Any red-zone value (RR 30 or more, SpO2 below his documented target, response only to pain or unresponsive), or new drowsiness or confusion, calls for a rapid response.

rows.note: Ambulance on scene: salbutamol given, O2 2 L/min NP started
ED triage: acute bay, monitor on, ECG done, bloods sent
Repeat set at bedside before medical review

handover.label: Arterial blood gas
handover.result: Arterial sample, right radial artery, collected 09:10 on 2 L/min oxygen by nasal prongs.
handover.model:
• Read: pH 7.37 (normal), PaCO2 52 mmHg (raised), HCO3 29 mmol/L (raised), base excess +3. PaO2 64 mmHg on 2 L/min (low). Lactate normal.
  • Meaning: hypoxaemia and hypercapnia, so type 2 respiratory failure. The normal pH with a raised bicarbonate means the hypercapnia is compensated, suggesting chronic CO2 retention (compare with any previous gas). There is no acute respiratory acidosis.
  • Changes: he is at risk of worse hypercapnia with too much oxygen, so keep SpO2 at 88 to 92% and use a spacer or air-driven nebulisers. NIV is not indicated now. Repeat the gas within about an hour, or sooner if he becomes drowsy. NIV is needed if pH falls below 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 mmHg despite treatment.

rows.n: on 2 L/min O2; range for room air

handover.label: Bloods
handover.result: Venous sample collected 09:05. Sputum sent for microscopy and culture: result pending.
handover.model:
• Read: WCC 13.2 with neutrophils 10.8 (both raised), CRP 42 (raised). Hb and platelets normal. Electrolytes, urea and creatinine normal, eGFR 68. Glucose 9.8 (raised, random). hs-troponin I 14 ng/L, below the male 99th percentile.
  • Meaning: an inflammatory response that fits a bacterial or viral trigger. A CRP of this level with no consolidation fits an exacerbation rather than pneumonia. No myocardial injury on this sample (against ACS); repeat hs-troponin at 2 to 3 hours per the ACS pathway. No anaemia contributing to the breathlessness.
  • Changes: supports antibiotics for the purulent sputum. Send a nasopharyngeal respiratory viral PCR (SARS-CoV-2, influenza, RSV) with droplet precautions until resulted; if he is COVID-positive, an antiviral is considered, avoiding nirmatrelvir/ritonavir with apixaban. Renal function allows standard doses and continuing apixaban. Withhold metformin while he is hypoxaemic and acutely unwell; restart when he has recovered. Monitor glucose and use correctional insulin once prednisolone starts.

handover.label: Chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, PA erect view. Mr Shawn Peters, 75, taken today at 09:40.

Clinical details: 75-year-old man with COPD and a heavy smoking history. Breathlessness since last night, much worse this morning, with wheeze and yellow sputum. Temperature 37.8 °C. SpO2 92% on 2 L/min. Query consolidation or pneumothorax.

Findings:

  • Technical: PA erect, not rotated, adequate penetration. Adequate inspiration.
  • Lungs: hyperinflated. Seven anterior ribs are visible above the right hemidiaphragm in the mid-clavicular line. Increased lucency in both upper zones with fewer vascular markings. Mild bronchial wall thickening at both bases. No focal consolidation. No mass or nodule.
  • Pleura: no pneumothorax. No pleural effusion. Costophrenic angles clear.
  • Heart and mediastinum: the heart is narrow and vertical, and not enlarged. Hila normal in size and position. Trachea central. No upper lobe venous diversion, septal lines or pulmonary oedema.
  • Diaphragm: both hemidiaphragms are low and flattened.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no acute bony abnormality.
  • Comparison: no previous imaging available.

Conclusion: hyperinflated lungs consistent with COPD. No consolidation, pneumothorax, effusion, pulmonary oedema or mass.
handover.model:
• Read: PA erect, adequate film. Hyperinflation: 7 anterior ribs, flattened hemidiaphragms, a narrow vertical heart, upper zone lucency. Mild bronchial wall thickening. No consolidation, pneumothorax, effusion, oedema or mass.
  • Meaning: changes of COPD, matching his hyper-resonance and wheeze. There is no pneumonia, no secondary pneumothorax and no heart failure to explain the exacerbation. No mass is seen, although a chest X-ray does not exclude early lung cancer.
  • Changes: treat as an exacerbation of COPD; no CT needed now. A persistent or new abnormality on a later film, or ongoing symptoms after recovery, would need further imaging.

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Shawn Peters, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Shawn now, here in the emergency department.
Before Shawn goes home after this admission, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, final-year medical student in ED; Shawn Peters, 75.
  • Situation: infective exacerbation of COPD. RR 26 and SpO2 92% on 2 L/min (yellow zone); SpO2 92% is already at the top of his 88 to 92% target, so the oxygen has not been increased. HR 106, BP 146/84, temperature 37.8 °C.
  • Background: COPD for 8 years with no previous admissions; MI with stent 2017, hypertension, T2DM; on apixaban, tiotropium and salbutamol; current smoker, about 50 or more pack-years; lives alone.
  • Assessment: unwell since last night, worse this morning; wheeze, yellow sputum; hyperinflated chest with widespread wheeze. ABG: compensated type 2 respiratory failure (PaCO2 52, pH 7.37), so he retains CO2 and must stay on controlled oxygen at 88 to 92%; no acidosis, so NIV is not needed now. WCC 13.2, CRP 42, troponin normal. CXR hyperinflation, no consolidation or pneumothorax.
  • Recommendation: please review and admit. Oxygen at 88 to 92%, bronchodilators, prednisolone and antibiotics started; repeat gas in an hour.

Infective exacerbation of COPD: subacute worsening, wheeze, yellow sputum, feels hot, heavy smoker, partly relieved by bronchodilator; widespread wheeze and hyperinflation; raised WCC and CRP with no consolidation.

  • Pneumonia: for: purulent sputum, 37.8 °C, CRP; against: no rigors, high fever or pleuritic pain, no focal signs or consolidation.
  • Secondary pneumothorax: for: COPD; against: symmetrical signs, none on CXR.
  • PE: for: tachycardia, hypoxaemia; against: on apixaban, no pleuritic pain, haemoptysis or calf swelling, infective picture.
  • Heart failure or ACS: for: previous MI, risk factors; against: tightness is respiratory in character (not crushing, no radiation), ECG sinus tachycardia with no acute change, first hs-troponin below the 99th percentile (repeat pending), no orthopnoea or oedema, JVP not raised, no oedema on CXR.
  • Lung cancer: for: smoking, mother's history; against: no weight loss or haemoptysis, no mass.

1. Senior ED review, monitoring, upright; controlled oxygen to SpO2 88 to 92% by nasal prongs or Venturi.
  2. Salbutamol 4 to 8 puffs (400 to 800 microgram) by spacer plus ipratropium 4 to 8 puffs (21 microgram per puff) by spacer, repeated (or nebulised by air: 2.5 to 5 mg and 500 microgram).
  3. Prednisolone 30 to 50 mg orally daily for 5 days; monitor BGL.
  4. Amoxicillin 500 mg 8-hourly for 5 days (or doxycycline 200 mg then 100 mg daily, 5 days in total).
  5. Repeat ABG within 1 hour; NIV if pH below 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 despite treatment; ICU if worsening.
  6. Admit; continue apixaban, withhold metformin.
  7. Extra credit, not required: sputum MCS, viral PCR, holding tiotropium, NRT, allied health.

• Explanation: a chest infection caused a flare-up of his COPD. A written COPD action plan, good inhaler technique and quitting smoking lower the chance of another one.
  • Smoking: acknowledge his grief; offer NRT and Quitline (13 7848).
  • Call 000: too breathless to talk, reliever not helping, blue lips, drowsy or confused, chest pain.
  • GP the same day: more or discoloured sputum, fever, needing the reliever more often.
  • Follow-up: GP within 7 days; pulmonary rehabilitation; vaccinations; personal alarm and his son's support.

ddx.dx: Infective exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
ddx.for: Known COPD in a heavy current smoker, with breathlessness worse since last night, wheeze, a new yellow sputum, feeling hot, partial relief from the paramedics' bronchodilator, widespread wheeze, raised WCC and CRP, and hyperinflation with no consolidation.
Purulent sputum, temperature 37.8 °C, and a raised WCC and CRP.
ddx.against: No high fever, rigors or pleuritic pain, no focal chest signs, and no consolidation on X-ray.

ddx.for: Known COPD with a sudden worsening of breathlessness.
ddx.against: No pleuritic pain, symmetrical expansion and breath sounds, trachea central, and no pneumothorax on X-ray.

ddx.for: Acute breathlessness with tachycardia and hypoxaemia.
ddx.against: Already anticoagulated with apixaban, no pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, immobility or calf swelling, and a clear infective, wheezy picture.

ddx.dx: Acute heart failure or acute coronary syndrome
ddx.for: Previous MI with a stent, with hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidaemia.
ddx.against: Tightness is respiratory in character (not crushing, no radiation), ECG sinus tachycardia with no acute change, first hs-troponin below the 99th percentile (repeat pending), no orthopnoea or oedema, JVP not raised, and no oedema on CXR.

ddx.for: Aged 75 with about 50 or more pack-years of smoking and a mother who had lung cancer.
ddx.against: No weight loss, night sweats, haemoptysis or clubbing, a subacute infective course, and no mass on X-ray.

guide:
In Part 1 the nurse gives the opening observations, including the paramedics' set on room air. Shawn answers in short, breathless sentences. Give the yellow sputum, wheeze and feeling hot only when the candidate asks about cough, sputum, wheeze or fever. Give examination findings only when the candidate says what they examine. If the candidate asks for the ECG, the nurse reports sinus tachycardia at about 106 with no acute changes. If they ask for other results, say these will be given in Part 2. If the candidate raises the oxygen to a "normal" target, play out the drowsiness in the script. Credit them if they recognise it and turn the oxygen back down.

In Part 2, hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order. Shawn asks his question after question 4 is read. Within their management answer, credit a candidate who mentions an ECG, sputum culture, a repeat troponin, or CTPA only if PE remains a concern despite his anticoagulation.

A high-performing candidate sets the oxygen target of 88 to 92% early. They characterise the breathlessness, elicit the change in sputum, screen pneumonia, heart failure, PE, ACS and malignancy, quantify the smoking and recognise that Shawn lives alone and is grieving. They percuss and auscultate both sides. In Part 2 they read the gas as compensated hypercapnia and link it to the oxygen target, exclude consolidation and pneumothorax on the X-ray, and prescribe bronchodilators, prednisolone and an antibiotic at the correct doses. They know the NIV criteria and arrange pulmonary rehabilitation and GP follow-up.

A borderline candidate takes a generic breathlessness history, misses the sputum change or the smoking, and does not percuss. They may call the gas normal because the pH is normal, or miss the hypercapnia. Giving high-flow oxygen to normal saturations, leaving out corticosteroids, or not having a plan for a rising CO2 is a serious safety concern.
explain:
Diagnosis: infective exacerbation of COPD

An exacerbation of COPD is a sustained worsening of symptoms beyond the usual day-to-day variation: more breathlessness, more sputum, and a change in sputum colour. It is most often triggered by a lower respiratory tract infection, commonly viral. Exacerbations can be fatal. Each one speeds the decline in lung function and lowers quality of life. Shawn has had COPD for 8 years with no previous exacerbations. He became unwell last night and woke extremely breathless, with a tight chest, wheeze and his usual dry cough now productive of yellow sputum. He felt hot and sweaty, and he is a heavy current smoker. The paramedics' inhaled bronchodilator helped him a little. The diagnosis is clinical: purulent cough, wheeze and rapid shallow breathing in a person with COPD. The investigations assess severity and exclude other causes.

The history

  • Characterise the episode: onset and course, character, severity (what he can no longer do), and response to treatment.
  • Exacerbation features: wheeze, a change in sputum volume or colour, fever and fatigue.
  • Exclude the differentials: pneumonia (high fever, rigors, pleuritic pain, sick contacts); heart failure (orthopnoea, PND, leg swelling, pink frothy sputum); PE (pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, immobility, calf swelling); ACS (central chest pain, radiation to the arm or jaw, nausea, palpitations); malignancy (night sweats, weight loss, poor appetite).
  • COPD severity: previous exacerbations, admissions, ICU or NIV, and baseline function.
  • Smoking: quantify it in pack-years. Shawn has smoked a pack a day since his early 20s, about 50 or more pack-years, and started again after his wife died.
  • Social context: he lives alone, is recently bereaved and depends on his son. This affects his disposition, his discharge planning and his mood.

The examination

Look for respiratory distress (tripod position, pursed lips, accessory muscles, tracheal tug), hyperinflation (barrel chest, reduced cricosternal distance, hyper-resonance, loss of cardiac dullness), and widespread wheeze with a prolonged expiratory phase. Pneumonia gives focal signs: bronchial breathing, focal crackles, dullness. A pneumothorax gives asymmetrical signs. Look for a CO2 retention flap and drowsiness, and for signs of heart failure (raised JVP, third heart sound, oedema).

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: the red-zone values at the scene improved with treatment. The yellow-zone RR and SpO2 call for a clinical review. In a patient who retains CO2, an SpO2 of 92% is already at the top of the target. Altered calling criteria should be documented so the chart reflects his target.
  • ABG: PaCO2 52 with a normal pH and a raised bicarbonate is compensated hypercapnia, suggesting chronic CO2 retention (compare with any previous gas). PaO2 64 on oxygen shows hypoxaemia. This is type 2 respiratory failure without acute acidosis. It confirms that high-concentration oxygen is dangerous: it can worsen hypercapnia and cause respiratory acidosis and drowsiness. A normal pH does not mean a normal gas.
  • Bloods: raised WCC and CRP fit an infective trigger. A first hs-troponin below the 99th percentile argues against ACS, but in a man with a previous MI a repeat at 2 to 3 hours is still needed under the ACS pathway. Normal renal function allows standard dosing. The raised glucose needs watching once corticosteroids start.
  • Chest X-ray: hyperinflation (more than 6 anterior ribs, flattened hemidiaphragms, narrow heart) with no consolidation, pneumothorax, oedema or mass.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia with no acute ischaemic change. Always record one in a patient with IHD.
  • Other tests: sputum for microscopy and culture, and a nasopharyngeal respiratory viral PCR (SARS-CoV-2, influenza, RSV), with droplet precautions until resulted. If he is COVID-positive, an antiviral is considered, avoiding nirmatrelvir/ritonavir because it interacts with apixaban. CTPA is considered only if PE remains a concern despite his anticoagulation with apixaban. Pneumonia can look similar but has more marked infective features and focal signs.

Management (COPD-X Plan, eTG Respiratory)

  1. Assess severity and escalate: monitoring, an upright position, and senior review.
  2. Controlled oxygen: target SpO2 88 to 92% (TSANZ, COPD-X), by nasal prongs or Venturi mask. Give nebulisers driven by air, or use an MDI with a spacer.
  3. Short-acting bronchodilators: salbutamol 400 to 800 micrograms by MDI and spacer, or 2.5 to 5 mg nebulised, repeated as needed. Add ipratropium 4 to 8 puffs (21 micrograms per puff) by MDI and spacer, or 500 micrograms nebulised (air-driven), repeated as needed, and withhold tiotropium while ipratropium is given regularly.
  4. Systemic corticosteroids: prednisolone 30 to 50 mg orally once daily for 5 days. They shorten recovery and reduce treatment failure. Monitor blood glucose in diabetes.
  5. Antibiotics when there are signs of infection such as purulent sputum: amoxicillin 500 mg orally 8-hourly for 5 days, or doxycycline 200 mg on day 1 then 100 mg daily for 4 days.
  6. Ventilatory support: repeat the ABG after changes in oxygen or if he becomes drowsy. NIV is indicated for an acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH below 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 mmHg) that persists despite optimal medical treatment. Involve ICU if he deteriorates or NIV fails.
  7. Disposition: admit. He needs oxygen, he has type 2 respiratory failure, he cannot walk to the toilet, and he lives alone. Continue his regular medicines (except tiotropium while regular ipratropium is given), including apixaban and the cardioselective beta-blocker metoprolol. Withhold metformin while he is acutely unwell and hypoxaemic, because of the risk of lactic acidosis (a normal first lactate does not change this), and restart it once he has recovered and is eating normally; monitor his BGL and use correctional insulin for steroid-induced hyperglycaemia. Offer NRT in hospital. Involve physiotherapy, OT, social work and his son.

Safety netting and follow-up

Shawn should leave with a written COPD action plan and checked inhaler technique. He needs to know to call 000 if he is too breathless to talk, his reliever is not helping, his lips turn blue, or he becomes drowsy, confused or has chest pain. He should see his GP the same day for more or discoloured sputum, fever or increasing reliever use. Arrange a GP review within 7 days of discharge and a referral to pulmonary rehabilitation, which reduces readmission after an exacerbation. Repeat spirometry when he is stable. Offer influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19 and RSV vaccination as recommended by the Australian Immunisation Handbook. Offer quit support (NRT, Quitline) with empathy for his grief, and bereavement and mood support. Because he lives alone, consider a personal alarm and his son's involvement, and when he is well, consider advance care planning. A chest X-ray does not exclude lung cancer: ongoing symptoms after recovery, weight loss or haemoptysis need further investigation.
points: In a person with COPD, more breathlessness with wheeze and a change in sputum colour or volume is an exacerbation until proven otherwise; actively exclude pneumonia, pneumothorax, PE and cardiac causes in the history, the examination and the X-ray.
Set the oxygen target to SpO2 88 to 92% before anything else, and drive nebulisers with air or use a spacer: too much oxygen in a CO2 retainer causes hypercapnic acidosis and drowsiness.
A normal pH does not mean a normal gas: a raised PaCO2 with a raised bicarbonate is compensated chronic hypercapnia. NIV is for pH below 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 mmHg despite optimal treatment.
Treat with repeated short-acting bronchodilators, prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days (watch the glucose in diabetes), and a 5-day oral antibiotic when the sputum is purulent.
Quantify smoking in pack-years and explore the social context: living alone, bereavement and a fear of another episode shape disposition, quitting and discharge planning.
Safety-net with a written COPD action plan, 000 red flags, GP review within 7 days, pulmonary rehabilitation, spirometry when stable, vaccination and quit support.
